results.title: Bayesian Model Comparison Essentials
results.content: In this guide, we will explore the essential techniques and best practices for Bayesian model comparison, including Bayes factors, posterior predictive checks, and cross-validation techniques. The techniques covered in this guide will provide a comprehensive understanding of Bayesian model comparison, enabling researchers to make informed decisions when evaluating model performance. ## Bayes Factors for Model Comparison. Bayes factors are a popular method for comparing the performance of different models in Bayesian statistics. Bayes factors can be interpreted as the relative evidence provided by the data for one model over another. ### Interpretation of Bayes Factors for Model Comparison. While Bayes factors are a powerful tool for model comparison, they have some limitations and challenges. * Using Bayes factors in conjunction with other model comparison techniques, like posterior predictive checks. ## Posterior Predictive Checks for Model Evaluation. Posterior predictive checks (PPCs) are a technique used to evaluate the performance of a Bayesian model by comparing the observed data to data simulated from the posterior predictive distribution. ## Cross-Validation Techniques for Bayesian Models. Cross-validation is a technique used to evaluate the performance of a model by splitting the available data into training and testing sets. ### Types of Cross-Validation Techniques for Bayesian Models. There are several types of cross-validation techniques that can be used for Bayesian models, including:. * **Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV)**: This involves leaving out one observation at a time and evaluating the model's performance on the remaining data. * **K-fold cross-validation**: This involves splitting the data into $K$ folds and evaluating the model's performance on each fold. These tools provide efficient and reliable methods for performing cross-validation and evaluating model performance. Suppose we want to compare the performance of two Bayesian linear regression models using cross-validation. By using techniques like Bayes factors, posterior predictive checks, and cross-validation, researchers can evaluate the performance of different models and identify the most suitable one for their data. Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Bayes factors are used to compare the relative evidence provided by the data for different models, while posterior predictive checks are used to evaluate the absolute fit of a single model to the data. ### Can I use Bayes factors with non-nested models?

results.title: Bayes factors evaluate priors, cross validations evaluate posteriors | Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science
results.content: # Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science # Bayes factors evaluate priors, cross validations evaluate posteriors I’ve written this explanation on the board often enough that I thought I’d put it in a blog post. Bayes factors compare the data density (sometimes called the “evidence”) of one model against another. Suppose we have two Bayesian models for data , one model with parameters and a second model with parameters The *Bayes factor* is defined to be the ratio of the marginal probability density of the data in the two models, The distributions and are known as *prior predictive distributions* because they integrate the likelihood over the prior. There are ad-hoc guidelines from Harold Jeffreys of “uninformative” prior fame, classifying Bayes factor values as “decisive,” “very strong,” “strong,” “substantial,” “barely worth mentioning,” or “negative”; see the Wikipedia on Bayes factors. The held out validation values are The distributions and are known as *posterior predictive distributions* because they integrate the likelihood over the posterior from earlier training data. Leave-one-out cross validation is interpretable as the expected log posterior density (ELPD) for a new data item. The main distinction between Bayes factors and cross validation is that the former uses prior predictive distributions whereas the latter uses posterior predictive distributions. This makes Bayes factors very sensitive to features of the prior that have almost no effect on the posterior. With hundreds of data points, the difference between a normal(0, 1) and normal(0, 100) prior is negligible if the true value is in the range (-3, 3), but it can have a huge effect on Bayes factors. The best way to get a good Bayes factor is to push the prior toward the posterior, which you get for free with cross validation. My question is whether the users of Bayes factors really believe so strongly in their priors. For more detail on these methods and further examples, see Gelman et al.’s *Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd Edition*, which is available free online through the link, particularly Section 7.2 (“Information criteria and cross-validation,” p. I’d also recommend Vehtari, Gelman, and Gabry’s paper, Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC.

results.title: Bayesian Model Selection: An In-Depth Guide
results.content: # Bayesian Model Selection: An In-Depth Guide. Rather than focusing solely on point estimates or p-values, Bayesian approaches incorporate prior knowledge and quantify uncertainty through the probability distribution of model parameters. In this guide, we walk through the key components of Bayesian model selection, including criteria for comparing models, practical steps in implementing these methods, and real-world case studies. We also provide insights into best practices in Bayesian model evaluation to help practitioners avoid common pitfalls and ensure responsible interpretation of results. Understanding the fundamental concepts behind Bayesian model selection is essential for any researcher or analyst interested in rigorous data analysis. Model evidence, or the marginal likelihood \(p(D \mid M)\), integrates the likelihood of the data over all possible parameter values weighted by the prior. In Bayesian contexts, k-fold cross-validation or leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) is used to estimate how well a model will perform on unseen data. Implementing Bayesian model selection can be streamlined using modern probabilistic programming languages like Stan and PyMC3. Use the generated log-likelihood values to compute model evidence estimates and employ criteria such as WAIC or DIC. Real-world case studies help illustrate the practical application of Bayesian model selection. flowchart TD A["Start: Define Models"] B["Compute Posterior Distributions"] C["Calculate WAIC/LOO"] D["Compare Evaluation Metrics"] E["Select Optimal Model"] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E. After conducting PSIS-LOO or WAIC analysis, Model 2 might provide improved predictions but be more sensitive to the choice of priors. Adhering to best practices ensures robust application of Bayesian model selection methods. Bayesian model selection offers a robust framework for comparing models by integrating prior knowledge with observed data. From understanding Bayes factors and model evidence to implementing practical solutions in Stan and PyMC3, the techniques discussed in this guide provide a comprehensive toolkit for applied statisticians and machine learning practitioners. * Multiple criteria, including DIC, WAIC, and cross-validation methods, help balance model fit with complexity. This comprehensive guide should serve as a valuable resource for understanding and applying Bayesian model selection in both academic and practical settings.

results.title: Chapter 12 Introduction to model comparison | Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis for Cognitive Science
results.content: There are two Bayesian perspectives on model comparison: a *prior* predictive perspective based on the Bayes factor using marginal likelihoods, and a *posterior* predictive perspective based on cross-validation. The main characteristic difference between the prior predictive approach (Bayes factor) versus the posterior predictive approach (cross-validation) is the following: The Bayes factor examines how well the model (prior and likelihood) explains the experimental data. In Bayes factor analyses, the prior model predictions are used to evaluate the support that the data give to the model. The posterior distributions of the parameters of this fitted model are then used to make predictions for held-out or validation data, and model fit is assessed on this subset of the data. According to Jaynes, Bayes factor adopts the posture of a cruel realist, who “judge[s] each model taking into account the prior information we actually have pertaining to it; that is, we penalize a model if we do not have the best possible prior information about its parameters, although that is not really a fault of the model itself.” By contrast, cross-validation adopts the posture of a scrupulously fair judge, “who insists that fairness in comparing models requires that each is delivering the best performance of which it is capable, by giving each the best possible prior probability for its parameters (similarly, in Olympic games we might consider it unfair to judge two athletes by their performance when one of them is sick or injured; the fair judge might prefer to compare them when both are doing their absolute best).”. 3. Model comparison is based on finding the most “useful model” for characterizing our data, but neither the Bayes factor nor cross-validation (nor any other method that we are aware of) guarantees selecting the model closest to the truth (even with enough data). Roberts and Pashler (2000) and Pitt and Myung (2002) argue for the need of going beyond “a good fit” (this is a good posterior predictive check in the context of Bayesian data analysis) and argue for the need of model comparison and a focus on measuring the generalizability of a model. (2023) uses \(17\) different data sets for model comparison using cross-validation, holding out each data set successively; this is an example of evaluating the predictive performance of a model on truly new data. “Bayesian Model Assessment and Comparison Using Cross-Validation Predictive Densities.” *Neural Computation* 14 (10): 2439–68. “A Survey of Bayesian Predictive Methods for Model Assessment, Selection and Comparison.” *Statistical Surveys* 6 (0): 142–228.

A novel procedure for obtaining cross-validated predictive estimates for Bayesian hierarchical regression models (BHRMs) is introduced, which circumvents the need to rerun computationally costly estimation methods for each cross-validation fold and makes CV more feasible for large BHRMs. The widely available information criterion (WAIC) and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) are considered fully Bayesian model selection methods due to their utilization of the whole posterior…. ### Conditional vs marginal estimation of the predictive loss of hierarchical models using WAIC and cross-validation. ### Unbiased estimator for the variance of the leave-one-out cross-validation estimator for a Bayesian normal model with fixed variance. Abstract When evaluating and comparing models using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV), the uncertainty of the estimate is typically assessed using the variance of the sampling distribution.…. ### Computational Methods for Fast Bayesian Model Assessment via Calibrated Posterior p-values. ### Limitations of Bayesian Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation for Model Selection. The limitations of a particular form of CV—Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation or LOO—are demonstrated with three concrete examples and it is concluded that CV is not a panacea for model selection. ### Bayesian Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation Approximations for Gaussian Latent Variable Models. ### Bayesian Model Assessment and Comparison Using Cross-Validation Predictive Densities. This work proposes an approach using cross-validation predictive densities to obtain expected utility estimates and Bayesian bootstrap to obtain samples from their distributions, and discusses the probabilistic assumptions made and properties of two practical cross- validate methods, importance sampling and k-fold cross- validation. ### Comparison of Bayesian predictive methods for model selection. The Bayes cross-validation loss is asymptotically equivalent to the widely applicable information criterion as a random variable and model selection and hyperparameter optimization using these two values are asymPTOTically equivalent.
